opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of it comes down to giving people ownership over questions they genuinely care about, rather than just handing them tasks. When I've built teams, one of the things I've found most important is creating space for researchers to identify the problems that feel urgent to them, and then making sure there's enough structure and support that they can actually make progress on those problems. Meaning doesn't come from being told your work matters; it comes from seeing the connection between what you're doing and something you believe is important.

I also care a lot about bringing in people with very different backgrounds. Some of the most interesting work I've been part of came from people who didn't follow the traditional path into machine learning. They ask different questions, they're less constrained by what the field assumes is settled, and that diversity of perspective makes the whole team sharper. It also makes people feel that their particular viewpoint is valued, which is a big part of finding your work meaningful.

And then there's the collaborative piece. Research can be very isolating, especially if the incentive structure rewards individual papers above everything else. I try to build an environment where people are genuinely invested in each other's success, where you get excited about a colleague's result, and where junior researchers get real mentorship and a chance to lead. When people feel like they're growing, and that they're part of something bigger than their own CV, that's when I see the most energy and the most ambitious work.

r001.rationale: The response links meaning to working with colleagues from varied backgrounds, feeling that one’s viewpoint is valued, and being part of a mutually supportive team.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is something I think about a lot, because I actually believe that meaning is one of the biggest levers you have as a research leader, and it's often treated as an afterthought.

The starting point for me is that researchers are incredibly motivated by the problem itself. People don't go into research to climb a ladder, they go into it because there's some question that keeps them up at night. So the first thing I try to do is make sure there's real alignment between what someone cares about and what the team is working on. That sounds obvious, but a lot of organizations do the opposite. They hire brilliant people and then slot them into whatever is strategically urgent that quarter, and you slowly watch the curiosity drain out of them.

The second thing is that meaning comes from being able to see the impact of your work. In machine learning right now, there's a real risk that research becomes very narrow. You optimize a benchmark by half a point, and you have no idea whether that matters to anyone. So I think a lot about connecting people to the downstream consequences. At Cohere For AI, a lot of our work touches on multilinguality, on efficiency, on who actually gets to use these models. When you're working with someone in a language community that has never had a model that works for them, the meaning is not abstract. It's very concrete, and that changes how people show up to the work.

The third piece is around how you structure teams. I'm a big believer in small teams with a lot of ownership. Researchers need to feel that their judgment matters, that they're not just executing someone else's plan. That means being deliberate about giving people a real stake in the direction, and being honest about tradeoffs rather than pretending there's one right answer. I also think diversity of perspective is huge here. Some of the most meaningful collaborations I've seen come from putting people together who have very different starting assumptions, because the friction forces everyone to articulate why they care about something.

And then the last thing, which is maybe less glamorous, is just the texture of day-to-day work. Does someone have time to think? Are they constantly fighting infrastructure? Do they feel safe saying that an idea isn't working? A lot of meaning gets eroded not by big strategic mistakes but by a thousand small frustrations. So part of my job is clearing that out of the way so people can actually do the thing they came here to do.

r001.rationale: The response says meaningful collaborations come from bringing together people with different starting assumptions, identifying collaborators as a source of meaning in research.

astra-6.text:
I think a lot of it starts with giving people ownership of the questions they’re working on. There’s a difference between being handed a task and understanding why a problem matters—and having a real say in how you approach it. Research involves so much uncertainty that you need that deeper motivation when something doesn’t work.

When I think about putting a team together, I also think about whether people bring different perspectives and whether they can actually learn from each other. You want enough shared purpose that people can move in a direction together, but enough room for someone to say, “I think we’re asking the wrong question.”

And then there’s the day-to-day environment. Can people share an early idea without feeling they have to defend a finished result? Do they feel their contributions are seen? Meaning isn’t something you establish once with a mission statement. It comes from having agency, growing through the work, and feeling that what you’re doing contributes to something you care about.

r001.rationale: The response says teammates should bring different perspectives and learn from each other, but it does not clearly identify the people researchers work with as a source of meaning.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot of it comes down to giving people ownership over the questions they’re working on. You want a shared sense of what matters and why, but you also want people to have room to shape the research. If every decision has already been made, it’s hard to feel that the work is yours.

And people find meaning in different ways. For one person, it might be understanding something fundamental; for another, it’s seeing someone actually use what they’ve built. So part of leading a team is listening and understanding what motivates each person, then connecting that to something the team can accomplish together.

You also need an environment where people can say, “I don’t understand this,” or, “I think we’re asking the wrong question.” Research involves uncertainty. People need to feel that an experiment that changes our thinking is valuable, even when it doesn’t produce the result we hoped for.

r001.rationale: The response discusses ownership, individual motivations, and shared team goals, but does not identify who researchers work with as a source of meaning.
